hints: Focus on the job title of the enzyme: DNA polymerase builds a new polymer strand, so ask yourself what units it is joining together.
Remember the two bond types in DNA: one holds the backbone of one strand together, the other holds the two strands to each other across the middle.
walkthrough:
**Recall what DNA polymerase does**

Think of DNA polymerase as the builder during DNA replication. It lines up free DNA nucleotides one by one against the template strand to make a new strand.

To make that strand, it must link nucleotide to nucleotide in a long chain.

**Pick the correct bond for the backbone**

Adjacent nucleotides in the same strand are joined by a strong covalent bond between the phosphate of one and the sugar of the next. That is called a phosphodiester bond.

Hydrogen bonds are different. They form spontaneously between complementary bases across the two strands, they are not made by DNA polymerase.

**Put bond and location together**

So we need phosphodiester (not hydrogen) and between nucleotides (to form the sugar-phosphate backbone, not between bases). That points straight to D.

options.A: Hydrogen bonds between bases do hold the two strands together, but they form by complementary base pairing, not by DNA polymerase action.
options.B: This mixes up the terms. Hydrogen bonds do not link nucleotides along a strand, they link bases across the two strands, and polymerase does not make them.
options.C: Phosphodiester is the right bond type, but it is never between bases. Bases pair by hydrogen bonds, while phosphodiester links sugar to phosphate.
options.D: Correct. DNA polymerase catalyses condensation reactions to form phosphodiester bonds between adjacent nucleotides, building the sugar-phosphate backbone of the new strand.
